title: High-rise window views: Evaluating the physiological and psychological impacts of green, blue, and built environments
research_question: 1. How do different elements of window views (greenery, water, urban landscapes) affect individuals' physiological well-being as measured by EEG, heart rate variability (HRV), skin conductance, and skin temperature? 2. How do these elements influence psychological well-being, including stress levels as assessed by the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI) and impression evaluation? 3. What combinations of window view elements most effectively promote overall well-being in high-rise environments?

participants.description: 45 doctoral and master's students (20 males, 25 females) from Tongji University, Shanghai, with mean ages of 27.58 ± 3.61 years (males) and 26.44 ± 4.82 years (females). All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no neurological disorders or psychoactive medication.
participants.recruitment: Online WeChat group and direct invitations

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six 4-minute aerial drone-captured videos (from 90m height) displayed on a 65-inch 4K Ultra HD monitor. Conditions: Control (C - gray screen), Urban architecture (B), Greenery (G), Mixed greenery and urban architecture (GB), Water bodies (W), Mixed greenery and water bodies (GW).

mechanisms: Green and blue spaces historically provided essential resources for survival, leading to innate positive emotional responses and enhanced well-being (evolutionary psychology).
Green and blue spaces help reduce mental fatigue and stress by offering restorative experiences, enhancing mood, and promoting relaxation (Attention Restoration Theory and Stress Reduction Theory).
Natural elements, especially greenery and water, enhance alpha brainwave activity, indicating greater relaxation and restful states.

Exposure to greenery and water increases parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity (indicated by increased SDNN, RMSSD, InHF, and decreased HR, LF/HF ratio), promoting physiological restoration and stress reduction.
Natural elements reduce sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activity (indicated by decreased SC), leading to lower emotional arousal and stress.
Integration of greenery with building views can mitigate the adverse effects of urban environments on physiological and psychological states.
implementation_implications: Urban planners and landscape designers should prioritize integration of green and blue spaces near high-rise buildings to enhance mental health and well-being.
Urban planning should employ a tailored approach for blue spaces, as varied impacts are observed; greatest benefits occur when green and water spaces are combined.
Even small patches of greenery interspersed between buildings can mitigate negative impacts of urban structures on mental well-being.

Architects should ensure green and blue spaces are visible from high-rise building windows to maximize physiological and psychological benefits, particularly in settings like hospitals, high-rise offices, and schools.

limitations: The study primarily involved young students, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
Future studies could include a broader demographic profile to enhance the applicability of the results.
The short duration of exposure to the landscape views may not fully capture the long-term effects of such environments on well-being; longitudinal studies with longer exposure periods are needed.
Although the use of video capture from a height of 90 m adds to the validity of our findings, actual exposure to real-life conditions might produce different results.
Future studies could explore the effects of live exposure to such views.
Investigating the impact of different architectural styles and the role of artificial green spaces could further enrich our understanding of how urban environments influence health.
